h1: Hospital software for the administrator who has to answer for the day.
sub: The administrator is asked about beds, money, staffing and complaints, usually in the same hour. HIMS puts occupancy, collections, departmental activity and rosters in one place, with the entry behind every figure still reachable.

sections.h2: What the administrator's job needs from a system
paras: An administrator does not use a hospital system the way a doctor or a billing clerk does. They are not entering data, they are answering for it. How many beds are free in the male ward, why did the pharmacy counter have a queue at noon, what has been collected today, who is on duty tomorrow evening, and who changed that bill. Those questions arrive in no particular order and usually need an answer before the next one arrives.

HIMS is useful here because every one of those answers comes from work the hospital has already done. Occupancy comes from bed management, collections from billing, departmental activity from the record the departments write to, rosters from the doctor schedule. Nothing is compiled, and because entries are attributed and timed, an administrator can go from a figure on the dashboard to the entry that produced it.

That last point matters more than it sounds. An administrator spends much of the day being told things by people who are busy, and a figure that can be opened down to the bill, the admission or the entry behind it is the difference between managing and mediating.

sections.h2: Most of the job is finding out what already happened.
sections.lead: Not because it is hidden, but because it is in four places and three of them are people.

items.p: Finding out how many beds are free means calling wards and adding up answers that are already stale.
The day's money is confirmed when the counter closes and the sheets are totalled.
Which department is busy is a matter of opinion because nobody produces comparable numbers.
Who is sitting when is a notice on a wall, and changes are communicated verbally.
A bill was altered or a discharge was delayed and there is no record of who did what, when.

items.q: Can I see occupancy without calling the wards?
items.a: Yes. Bed management shows every ward and bed as it currently stands, updated by the admissions, transfers and discharges the wards are already recording. See bed management.

items.q: Can I control what each staff member can see?
items.a: Access is role based, so front desk, nursing, pharmacy, billing and management each see what their role allows. The roles are configured at setup and changed as your team changes.

items.q: Is there an audit trail behind a bill or a record?
items.a: Entries are attributed to the user and timed, and bills carry an audit trail, so a disputed charge or an altered record can be traced rather than argued about.
Doctor rosters and consulting days are held in the system and drive the appointment book and the token queues, so a change to who is sitting when reaches the front desk rather than a notice board.

items.q: How is this different from the owner's view?
items.a: The owner wants the headline daily. An administrator needs to act on it during the day and reach the entry behind it. Same platform, different depth. See the owner dashboard.

items.q: How long before we are running on it?
items.a: The scope is fixed at the start and the target is live in 30 working days where that scope allows, including migration of your existing data and training at your own counters.

items.p: The whole hospital on one platform.
